I went to court with my son last week for a trial for some tickets that he had got for something that he did not do. He got tickets for vandalism, curfew violation and obstruction. Apparently he was at his mothers house, and their neighbor called the police one morning and informed them that someone had poured maple syrup and chili powder all over his pickup truck. So the police officer comes to the scene. He looks at the truck and scans the area and he sees a maple syrup bottle in my x-wifes yard. He goes to the door and my son answers, the cop asks my son if he knows anything about the incident. My son tells him that he doesn't know anything about it. The cop talks to my x, asks her what brand of syrup she uses, where she keeps her maple syrup and if he can see it. She says I don't know and lets the cop look in her fridge and her cupboard, where he doesn't find any syrup. So the cop writes the three citations to my son.

Now my son swears to me that he did not do this, and that he does not know who did. He was inside playing video games and sleeping overnight, I tend to believe him, so we plead not guilty and are set for a trial by judge.

So the trial comes, and the cop gets on the witness stand and tells the story about finding the bottle and not finding syrup in the house. I didn't hire a lawyer cause these are all $50 dollar fines and not really worth the expense, so I ask the court if I may represent my son and ask questions of the officer. They all agree to allow this. So I ask the officer if he has any witnesses or reports of my son having been out after curfew. He says no. I ask what evidence do you have of him being out after curfew. He has none. OK great, I feel I have made my point there and move on to the next subject. I ask the cop if he did any fingerprint analysis of the bottle to prove who had handled it. He says no, that he would have to send it to the crime lab and that would take months and cost a lot of money. So I ask him what evidence he has that my son had anything to do with the incident. The cop proceeds to mention that on a later date he talked to another youth, who he would not name, and that youth had made a claim that my son was involved. I ask the cop, where is this witness, I would like to question him. He says that the witness is not here, but he has a signed statement from him, that I can not see because it contains his name.

At this time I bring up the point that the statement is inadmissible. I can not question a piece of paper. If they want to use that kids statement against my son that he needs to be in court to make that statement. Now the judge stops the proceedings and threatens me with contempt of court. I don't know why, but he does. So I stop making this point and ask if I may resume my questions. He allows me to continue questioning. Now I ask the cop if it would be reasonable to assume that someone may have had a beef with the neighbor and came from somewhere else to pour the syrup and chili powder on his truck and simply threw the bottle in the yard as they made their escape. The cops tells me that I am making some profound leaps of judgement there. So I ask him, if someone were to shoot your neighbor and happened to toss the gun into your yard as they were leaving the scene would that make you guilty of murder?

Now everyone in the courtroom is talking at once and the judge threatens me again with contempt of court. He looks at me and says there are two officers in this room and I can have either one of them put handcuffs on you right now if you wish. So after that threat I agree to stop this line of questioning and move on. I have one last question for the cop. Knowing my son and knowing him not to lie to me when pressed for the truth, what evidence does the officer have to give my son and obstructing ticket when my son told you that he knows nothing at all about an incident that he was not involved in. The cop says. I believe that he was involved in the truck incident and therefor I believe that he is lying to me. I state that it takes more than belief to charge someone with a crime in America and this is a court of law. With that I stop asking questions.

I felt like I had made my points fairly well, raised a reasonable doubt and pointed out the fact that they had no evidence at all against my son.

The judge has made his decision.

He says, that because we did not prove that my son did not do this act, that he is going to side with the police and find him guilty of all three charges, we now owe $185 due to the court costs being added to the fines. I said to the judge, this is America, the burden of proof is on the prosecution, not the defense. We do not have to prove that he did not do it, you have to prove that he did. This is where I was threatened with contempt of court for the third time. I looked around the room silently, said excuse me, and told me son I am leaving, you finish this. and left the room. I really didn't want to go to jail for this farce of a trial.

I just had to get that off my chest, and I wonder what you guys think. Should we appeal this decision? Or just pay the money and move on?

Courts actually differ from state to state, but some common things I do know about how juvenile courts are different:

  1. Juveniles are prosecuted for delinquent acts. not crimes. If the delinquent act is very serious, they are charged as adults as a crime.

  2. Juveniles don't have a right to a public trial by jury. If a kid is charged, the trial part is a judge hearing evidence and ruling on whether or not the kid is delinquent. It's called an adjudication hearing.

  3. If the court finds a kid delinquent, the court will determine the action. This stage differs from the adult system in that in Juvenal systems it is not supposed to be punishment like an adult, rather it is supposed to be rehabilitation. The reality of that is up for debate I am sure.

  4. Juvenile courts are often more informal than those for adults. For example, rules about the admissibility of evidence may be more lenient.

As far as the rights of a kid:

  • The right to an attorney
  • The right to confront and cross-examine witnesses
  • The privilege against self-incrimination
  • The right to notice of the charges
  • The prosecution must provide proof beyond a reasonable doubt before a person can be convicted

The point is the court proceedings are different than an adult so knowing where the OP was off with the procedures, without having a Juvenal lawyer from that state, is hard to know.

Generally, if you want to get into legal activism (please do, there are so few of us left that actually fight for rights), you need to have your entire plan laid out in advance, and be in control of the pacing from the beginning. They brought charges on your son that you weren't expecting. They already gained control of the pacing, and you are playing defense (pun intended).

If you suddenly had the fire lit inside of you, and feel you want to do something 'real' for your freedoms, then I have some tips and suggestions in no particular order:

1) Proceed according to your shotclock, not theirs. That is, if you want to fight something unconstitutional, you don't want to first be charged, and then decide to fight it as a constitutional issue. You first lay your entire plan out, and then you need to get charged with the offense you want to challenge. This makes some laws harder to fight than others, as some egregious offenses are hard to be intentionally charged with. Furthermore, if you develop a reputation, savvy prosecutors will intentionally sit on your case, or savvy judges will intentionally dismiss your case because of some contrived technicality.

2) Every state has a different court setup, with different rights and procedures. It is absolutely worth your time to find and read both the law, and the procedures. The latter is the most important, as procedure varies a lot from county to county, let alone from state to state. Additionally, court procedure is hidden in many counties/states, and used to distinguish those who 'know the system' from those who don't. Proper procedure is key, I can't state this enough.

3) Generally, the inferior courts (usually called 'district courts' or similar) are the kangaroo courts of any state. This is where you find courts not of record, where you have 'no right to discovery', where 'trials by judge' take place and civil-criminal hybrid 'infractions' abound, and so forth.

4) What you call a 'trial by judge' is sometimes called a 'bench trial', or 'magistrates court'. Essentially, the judgement on your case is at the whim of one man. You can always get a jury trial (even if you are not 'allowed' to, see list at the bottom of current issues), but it is usually a moot point, as judges can overrule juries in many jurisdictions (completely serious, reread this to let it sink in). Bench trials are always a de facto conflict of interest for the judge, and this is the most common angle of attack that activists use to force jury trials.

5) Representation and counsel are not the same thing. Your right to counsel is constitutionally protected, but only an attorney may 'represent' you. This is why I need to make no disclaimer about legal advice.

6) Similar to the importance of procedure, from earlier: form over function. A very prolific but now deceased legal activist used to frequently say "show them the paper that they want to see, and they will show you the paper that you want to see". That is, any paper you file - be it a motion, affidavit, or otherwise - should be identical in appearance to the convention that your court uses. Look online (or in person) and study the formatting of the motions, and format yours to match. In an ideal world, you are protected by 'pro-se leniency' (case law for this at the end), but in reality, your knowledge of form and procedure is used to judge your 'weight class'.

7) Make them play by their own rules. This involves first learning the rules, from earlier.

8) Be very careful with your words; legal jargon borrows many words from common vernacular, but doesn't share the same meanings. Precision is key. Legal dictionaries are a must.

9) Be aware that the 'law' isn't just what you can read in your articles and ordinances (called 'statutory law'); 'law' also includes case law (which has incredible depth and breadth). I once had a judge in a bench trial tell me that the law of my state provides me no right to discovery in district court - he assumed I thought (like most laymen would) that statutory law is all of applicable law - his demeanor changed when I calmly provided him recent case law establishing I did in fact have that right. Read the case law, but make sure it is applicable. It must be from your state, a ruling from your state's supreme court trumps a contradictory ruling from an appellate court, and newer cases trump older ones.

10) Courts are public spaces. That is, though you may not be able to find cases online, you can examine the file from any case in any court in this country for free, and usually make copies for a small fee. The trick is to know which cases are of interest. Many states allow you to search slip opinions online, but when you find an interesting opinion, you will usually need to go to the courthouse to 'get the whole story'.

11) You should seek out and understand with vigor all of the implicit 'opt-out' aspects of law. An decent example is objection; if you do not object when you can (and the judge does not see fit to object on your behalf), then you waive your right to object in the future. The flaw with implicit agreements is huge: if you don't know that you could have objected, you are still assumed to have been competent enough to know you could have objected, and instead chose not to, thereby waiving your right.

 

That is all for now, it is late and I have been at this too long. And now, a synopsis of current legal activism: Most legal activism is on the West Coast, unfortunately. Many great battles have been quietly won there, and many citizens on the West Coast now enjoy rights that we on the East Coast didn't even know we lost. Examples of great battles won or ongoing against an encroaching police state:

-California: U.S. v Colin establishes that weaving and lane straddling is not probable cause to pull someone over. Although this case is very versatile, it is currently being used primarily to destroy DUI cases. It has been successfully imported into other states with similar wording of their statutes.

-California: California has no 'inferior' court - the kangaroo courts of California have been entirely abolished. My mentors in this field say the inferior courts were singlehandedly destroyed by one man, but this happened over 40 years ago and the web has been entirely whitewashed on the issue.

-Washington: A group of legal activists found a way to attack unmarked police vehicles (as unreasonable search and seizure, iirc). They have the plan, but no way to execute yet; they are currently looking for a suitable case where someone was ticketed from an unmarked police vehicle.

-Washington: King county (where Seattle is located) is a locus for corruption, and it pervaded the Seattle 'justice' system thoroughly and entirely. The crux was prosecutorial immunity - essentially, a prosecutor has very few controls (I know of only two), and they only come into effect if extreme conditions are reached. King County prosecutors were using their immunity to commit perjury to win their cases. Kalina v. Fletcher was a massive smack across the face of King County, and now prevents WA prosecutors from committing perjury as a third control (in addition to vindictive or malicious prosecution, the only other 2 controls I know of).

-Washington: A group of legal activists are currently planning a case against King County, as it seems King County is running a property theft ring that doubles as an animal sex brothel (you can't make this stuff up).
